newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling slips on shortfall in export income.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling slips on shortfall in export income.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling suffered further losses after news of a shortfall in expected dollar inflows from agricultural exporters, commercial dealers said on Tuesday.
The market remained calm but nervous and the besieged shilling was expected to be under further pressure on Wednesday.
Foreign exchange dealers said the shilling slid 2.2 percent to close at 63.60/64.90 by Tuesday mid-afternoon after holding stable for most of the day at 62.50/63.50.
The latest losses meant the shilling has depreciated by a total of 9.07 percent since Friday's opening.
"People were expecting coffee and tea monies in the afternoon and so they were in short dollar positions in anticipation of the dollar inflows," one dealer told Reuters.
"The coffee and tea money which came in was too little."
Dealers estimated about $2 million came in from weekly auctions attended by coffee exporters while just below $250,000 came in from tea exporters. The coffee and tea inflows were quickly lapped up.

Bidders at Kenya's weekly coffee export auctions, who fly into Nairobi for from the coastal city of Mombasa, were delayed by an air traffic control go-slow at Kenyan airports and the auction began late, coffee dealers told Reuters.
Dealers said the sudden movement in the afternoon only served to aggravate an already nervous market.

"This gives the direction for the coming day and makes the market more nervous. Come Wednesday the effects will be felt in the morning," a dealer said. The dealer said some investors quoted a shilling price of as little 65 against the dollar and got paid.
Earlier on Tuesday, the shilling had settled warily after the central bank sold dollars to commercial banks to enable nervous offshore investors to get out of the market.

Commercial bank dealers said the central bank (CBK) sold up to $21 million to meet orders from foreign investors who wanted to disinvest from government treasury bills in the aftermath of an IMF decision to cancel a key aid package to Kenya.

The IMF ruling last week in a row over corruption rocked the foreign exchange and equity markets and sent the shilling plummeting to levels as low as 64.50 -- the lowest since October 1993 when it touched 69 to the dollar.
The shilling rebounded to 61.50 on Friday but suffered further losses on Monday, sliding 3.35 percent to 63.50 on heavy dollar demand from nervous foreign investors.
Some dealers said the CBK intervention helped calm the market by showing that the central bank was prepared and able to meet foreign demand for dollars when the need arose.
"It was good the central bank came in. Otherwise the shilling would have collapsed," a dealer told Reuters.
Last week Kenyan Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said that the government would let market forces determine shilling direction but it still hoped to maintain price stability.

The Kenyan cabinet on Monday appeared to rule out a quick return to negotiations with the International Monetary Fund, saying that Kenyans must depend on themselves to develop their country. But the cabinet also asked for investors to stay calm.

President Daniel arap Moi, aged 73 and in power since 1978, faces elections this year pitting the KANU party against an opposition that has found fragile cohesion in a campaign for constitutional reform. No election date has been set.
